values.goal: Understand WGSL types, stage interfaces, address spaces, memory layout, and parallel control flow, and write verifiable kernels.
values.capstone: A small compute collection that verifies bounds, layout, and synchronization, and a comparison report against CPU references

values.title: Types and Entry Points
values.prerequisites: WebGPU buffers and pipelines, and vector operations
values.environment: The existing wgsl-01 preview is a starting point. It does not replace implementation or verification of the full subsequent assignment. This document-guided exercise requires your own implementation in a separate localhost or HTTPS project. Check the secure context, navigator.gpu, and adapter request result, and provide an unsupported-environment message. Retain device.lost handling and resource cleanup.
values.concepts.0.title: Stage Contracts
values.concepts.0.explanation: @vertex, @fragment, and @compute specify the shader stage in which a function runs. Each stage permits different inputs, outputs, and builtins.
values.concepts.1.title: Identifying Inputs and Outputs
values.concepts.1.explanation: @location specifies an interface location for user data, while @builtin passes a system-defined value. These attributes cannot be interchanged by simply renaming them.
values.outcomes.0: Write the input and output contract for each stage.
values.steps.0: In shader.wgsl, write an @vertex function that generates triangle positions using vertex_index.
values.steps.1: Return @builtin(position) and a @location(0) color in a structure, and receive them in the fragment stage.
values.steps.2: Introduce a location type mismatch, inspect getCompilationInfo and pipeline errors, and restore the correct types.
values.variables.0.name: Color location
values.variables.0.expected: A mismatch is expected to appear during stage linkage validation.
values.criteria.0: Explain builtin and location inputs in two items each.
values.criteria.1: Distinguish diagnostics for valid source from diagnostics for erroneous source.
values.questions.0: Can the position builtin be replaced with an ordinary location?
values.questions.1: How does vertex_index differ from vertex buffer attributes?
values.references.0.title: WGSL Specification
values.references.1.title: WebGPU API

values.concepts.0.title: Abstract Numbers
values.concepts.0.explanation: A literal without a fixed type can resolve to a concrete type according to its context. Make the intended f32, i32, or u32 explicit at variable and function boundaries.
values.concepts.1.title: Conversions
values.concepts.1.explanation: Signed and unsigned integers have different ranges and operation semantics. Make conversions between indices and computed values explicit to avoid interpreting values unexpectedly.
values.steps.0: In types.wgsl, write i32, u32, and f32 variables and explicit conversion functions.
values.steps.1: Record positive, negative, and fractional inputs in a small compute output buffer.
values.steps.2: Create an error case that directly adds different concrete types, then compare the results after conversion.
values.variables.0.name: Input type
values.variables.0.expected: The fractional part of the result and the available conversions are expected to differ.
values.criteria.0: Tabulate the ranges and uses of the three types.
values.criteria.1: Record the mixed-type error and three values after correction.
values.questions.0: Can converting a negative value to u32 replace input validation?
values.questions.1: How does type resolution differ for the literals 1 and 1u?

values.concepts.0.title: Vector Construction
values.concepts.0.explanation: vec2f, vec3f, and vec4f group components for computation. Distinguish the rules for reading and writing swizzles.
values.concepts.1.title: Matrix Semantics
values.concepts.1.explanation: WGSL matrices consist of column vectors. The column order written by the CPU must match the shader's matrix multiplication for the intended transformation.
values.steps.0: In math.wgsl, create functions that output vector construction, swizzle, and dot results.
values.steps.1: Choose the two columns of a mat2x2f and a vec2f input, and calculate their product by hand.
values.steps.2: Use readback to compare results from the correct input and an input with the CPU array order changed.
values.variables.0.name: Matrix columns
values.variables.0.change: Array with rows and columns swapped
values.variables.0.expected: A nonsymmetric matrix is expected to produce a different transformation.
values.criteria.0: Record expected values for four vector and matrix operations.
values.criteria.1: The GPU result for a nonsymmetric matrix matches the hand calculation.
values.questions.0: Why is it difficult to find row and column errors using only diagonal matrices?
values.questions.1: What are the return types of vector multiplication and dot?

values.concepts.0.title: Mutability
values.concepts.0.explanation: const and let express values that are not reassigned, but differ in evaluation time. Use var for state that changes during function execution.
values.concepts.1.title: Pipeline Constants
values.concepts.1.explanation: override defines a value that can be supplied when creating a pipeline. A resource such as a uniform is more suitable than override for inputs that change every frame.
values.outcomes.0: Choose declarations that match value lifetimes.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish pipeline constants from runtime inputs.
values.steps.0: In constants.wgsl, distinguish a const coefficient, a let intermediate value, and a var accumulator.
values.steps.1: Set override SCALE to 1 and 2 through pipeline constants.
values.steps.2: Inspect a let reassignment error and move per-frame color input into a uniform.
values.variables.0.name: SCALE
values.variables.0.expected: The pipeline's result is expected to double, with a lifetime different from a uniform update.
values.criteria.0: Tabulate when the four declarations are evaluated and can change.
values.criteria.1: Record the results for two pipeline constants and the let reassignment error.
values.questions.0: Why does changing override require a different pipeline configuration?
values.questions.1: Which declaration suits a value that stays unchanged during a function call?

values.concepts.0.title: Separating Functions
values.concepts.0.explanation: Separating pure computation functions makes it easier to verify the same mathematics in vertex and compute stages. Declare concrete input and return types.
values.concepts.1.title: Structures
values.concepts.1.explanation: Structures group related fields, but stage attributes and memory conventions depend on where a structure is used. Do not assume a screen input/output structure is also a storage structure.
values.outcomes.0: Create computation functions with explicit types.
values.steps.0: In functions.wgsl, write wave(x,time,amplitude) and a result structure.
values.steps.1: Pass five x inputs to the function from a compute entry point and output the results.
values.steps.2: Use the same function for vertex displacement, then compare the numeric output and maximum displacement.
values.variables.0.name: Amplitude
values.variables.0.expected: The wavelength is expected to remain unchanged while maximum displacement triples.
values.criteria.0: The CPU and WGSL function values differ by no more than 1e-5 for five inputs.
values.criteria.1: Separate the inputs of stage functions and pure computation functions.
values.questions.0: Should stage attributes be attached to ordinary computation function arguments?
values.questions.1: Does splitting functions always increase GPU call overhead?

values.concepts.0.title: Control Flow
values.concepts.0.explanation: if, switch, for, and loop express computation paths and iteration counts. Set an upper bound when connecting termination conditions to inputs to prevent unexpectedly long work.
values.concepts.1.title: Branch Semantics
values.concepts.1.explanation: select is different from an ordinary short-circuiting if. Do not hide unsafe memory access in one of select's arguments.
values.steps.0: In flow.wgsl, write an accumulating for loop with an upper bound of 8 and a mode switch.
values.steps.1: Use if to branch before buffer access when the length is insufficient.
values.steps.2: Compare the results for two modes and iteration counts 0, 1, and 8 with a CPU function.
values.variables.0.name: Iteration count
values.variables.0.expected: The accumulated result and workload are expected to increase; 0 is expected to return the initial value.
values.criteria.0: The results for six combinations match the CPU reference.
values.criteria.1: Array bounds checks do not depend on select argument evaluation.
values.questions.0: Can you assume that only one of the two expressions in select is evaluated?
values.questions.1: What problems arise if loop termination depends only on external data?

values.concepts.0.title: Interpolation Rules
values.concepts.0.explanation: Floating-point vertex outputs are interpolated in the fragment stage. Integer identifiers must explicitly use flat interpolation.
values.concepts.1.title: System Coordinates
values.concepts.1.explanation: The vertex position output and fragment position input do not represent the same coordinates. Check screen coordinate conventions when using fragment positions.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish the meanings of system coordinates.
values.steps.0: In interface.wgsl, output both a color and an integer id with @interpolate(flat).
values.steps.1: Display id-based colors and interpolated colors in separate fragment modes.
values.steps.2: Compare screen UVs obtained by normalizing fragment position by resolution with vertex UVs.
values.variables.0.name: Color interpolation
values.variables.0.expected: Color variation inside the triangle is expected to disappear, filling it with the value from the designated vertex.
values.criteria.0: Explicitly specify flat interpolation for an integer location.
values.criteria.1: Compare the two modes: screen position and vertex UV.
values.questions.0: When do perspective interpolation and linear screen interpolation differ?
values.questions.1: Why must you check which vertex supplies the flat value?

values.concepts.0.title: Address Spaces
values.concepts.0.explanation: function, private, workgroup, uniform, and storage determine value lifetimes and sharing scopes. Even similar-looking names have different sets of invocations that can access them.
values.concepts.1.title: Write Permissions
values.concepts.1.explanation: Writing to a uniform or read-only storage violates its contract. Specify storage read or read_write access according to the actual operation.
values.steps.0: In spaces.wgsl, declare a read-only uniform, read storage, and a read_write output.
values.steps.1: Add comments distinguishing a function-local accumulator from a private variable.
values.steps.2: Create an error by writing to a read-only input, then restore the code by writing to the output.
values.variables.0.name: Input access
values.variables.0.change: Attempt to write to the input
values.variables.0.expected: Validation or shader diagnostics are expected to reveal the contract violation.
values.criteria.0: Tabulate the sharing scopes of the five address spaces.
values.criteria.1: Write results to a separate output without changing the read-only input.
values.questions.0: Is a private variable shared by all invocations?
values.questions.1: Can workgroup memory be used in the same way in the fragment stage?

values.concepts.0.title: Resource Locations
values.concepts.0.explanation: @group and @binding specify resource connection locations in the shader. Even with matching numbers, texture, sampler, and buffer types must satisfy the host contract.
values.concepts.1.title: Minimum Size
values.concepts.1.explanation: A buffer binding must contain enough data for the shader to read. Check both the bind group layout's minimum size and the actual binding range.
values.outcomes.0: Connect resource locations to the host.
values.steps.0: In bindings.wgsl, declare a color uniform in group 0 and a storage array in group 1.
values.steps.1: In host.js, write two bind group layouts and the corresponding resources.
values.steps.2: Use error scopes to check cases with an incorrect binding number, visibility, or buffer type, one at a time.

values.questions.0: Does a group number represent a memory address?
values.questions.1: Does automatic layout remove validation of shader and resource types?

values.concepts.0.title: Alignment and Size
values.concepts.0.explanation: Alignment constrains the multiples at which a starting address can occur; size is the space occupied by the data. Distinguish vec3f alignment 16 from size 12 to calculate the next member's position.
values.concepts.1.title: Member Offsets
values.concepts.1.explanation: Round each member's start up from the previous end to its own alignment. Round the entire structure size up to the structure's alignment as well.
values.outcomes.1: Match byte writes to shader interpretation.
values.steps.0: In layout.md, calculate offsets 0, 16, and 28 for a:f32,b:vec3f,c:f32 and a total size of 32.
values.steps.1: Use DataView to write values at these byte offsets and create a storage buffer.
values.steps.2: Copy the three fields into separate output positions in compute and read them back.
values.variables.0.name: b offset
values.variables.0.expected: b and c are expected to be read incorrectly because the positions differ from those expected by the shader.
values.criteria.0: The table of each member's alignment, size, and offset is correct.
values.criteria.1: All components read from the correct layout match the input.
values.questions.0: Does an f32 after a vec3 always occur 16 bytes later?
values.questions.1: What changes if trailing structure padding is ignored in an array?

values.concepts.0.title: Matrix Layout
values.concepts.0.explanation: mat3x3f stores three vec3f columns at aligned intervals. Although there are nine values, its storage layout differs from a simple contiguous 36-byte array.
values.concepts.1.title: Array Spacing
values.concepts.1.explanation: An array element's stride is its size rounded up to its alignment. Use the same stride when moving to the next element on the CPU.
values.steps.0: In matrix-layout.md, record mat3x3f column offsets 0, 16, and 32 and size 48.
values.steps.1: Write two matrices with a 48-byte stride and multiply each by a different vector.
values.steps.2: Compare normal readback results with a case incorrectly written at 36-byte intervals.
values.variables.0.name: Matrix stride
values.variables.0.expected: The second matrix and the values in each column are expected to be misaligned.
values.criteria.0: Record padding for the three columns and starting positions of the two elements.
values.criteria.1: The results for two nonsymmetric matrices match the CPU reference.
values.questions.0: Which padding errors can be missed if you test only mat4x4f?
values.questions.1: Are array stride and dynamic binding offset the same value?

values.concepts.0.title: Uniform Rules
values.concepts.0.explanation: Additional layout constraints may apply to arrays and nested structures in the uniform address space. For a baseline compatible path, design array spacing in units of 16 bytes and check the rules actually supported.
values.concepts.1.title: Explicit Padding
values.concepts.1.explanation: Matching padding declarations in the host and shader can produce a compatible layout. @size and @align do not automatically create the host bytes.
values.outcomes.1: Reflect explicit padding in the host.
values.steps.0: In uniform-array.wgsl, write an Element structure with a @size(16) value:f32 member and a fixed-size array.
values.steps.1: In host.js, use DataView to place each value 16 bytes apart.

values.criteria.1: The four values update independently in the compatible layout.
values.questions.0: Can storage and uniform arrays be assumed to have the same layout?
